Marketplace®

Donate
Nov 6, 2026
Latest jobs report shows a white-collar hiring turnaround
The U.S. economy added 165,000 jobs in October. One surprising growth spot was in professional and business services, which accounted for about 70,000 of those job gains.
Workplace/Jobsby Elizabeth Trovall
Download
An uptick in professional and business services jobs could indicate a shift in firms' AI outlook.
Joe Raedle/Getty Images
The October jobs report, out Friday, looks rosy for a number of sectors. The U.S. economy added 165,000 new jobs last month, while unemployment ticked slightly down to 4.1%.
It’s another sign that strength in the U.S. economy is broadening, said Yelena Shulyatyeva, senior U.S. economist at The Conference Board.
“If you look at the labor market, you see strength in both goods and services producing sectors,” she said.
Manufacturing employment increased, for example.
Healthcare is another growing sector, said Andrew Flowers, chief economist at recruitment technology firm Appcast. He said that’s no surprise.
"[Healthcare] has been a stalwart industry for job growth,” he said. “The other is the kind of standing up, hard hat industries of transportation. All these industries that I would say related to the AI data center build out those add jobs as well.”
Still, there were some surprises in the jobs report.
“The third industry that added jobs — and it was such a surprise — is professional and business services. This is a real reversal of the white collar bloodbath we've seen over the past few years,” Flowers said.
Some of those new roles are also connected to AI, said Bill Driscoll with talent and consulting firm Robert Half.
“Where companies thought they might be able to replace folks with AI. Now, increasingly, they're they're wanting folks that can interact with AI and provide judgment [and] communication insights in conjunction with AI,” he said.
Driscoll is also seeing employers looking to fill corporate positions in security and data.
“Anytime you're seeing a lot of data work, that's cleaning up your data to prepare to be able to use AI, and then obviously security is a huge deal right now,” he said.
Those roles are more likely to be mid to higher level jobs. Though Driscoll said the entry level market is also loosening up a bit as companies think about their future workforce.

What you should know about the new I Bond rate and the Treasury's new login process
Marketplace®
Every story is an economic story
Donate
Nov 6, 2026
What you should know about the new I Bond rate and the Treasury's new login process
I Bonds purchased between now and April 2027 are paying an annual rate of 5.51%, the highest rate since 2022. But the Treasury is now using ID.me, third-party service that has raised privacy and security concerns.
Financial Healthby Janet Nguyen
The new I Bond rate comes with a new way of logging in.
jetcityimage/Getty Images
The Treasury Department has announced that I Bonds, which are considered inflation-proof investments, will start paying an annual interest rate of 5.51%, if you purchase them between now and April.
Since the early years of the pandemic, I Bonds have become a more attractive investment vehicle as inflation has risen. In 2022, they offered a record 9.62% interest rate rate.
While the rate has dipped since then, the rate is now the highest it's been since November 2022. But those trying to buy I Bonds will encounter a new system they have to navigate: ID.me, a third-party service that has raised concerns from lawmakers and experts.
Here's what you should know about these investments and using ID.me.
How I Bonds work
The interest rate on I Bonds are based on a fixed rate, which remains the same rate you bought it at throughout its 30-year lifespan, and an inflation rate, which is based on the Consumer Price Index and changes every six months. Because the inflation rate changes every six months, so does your overall rate.
I Bonds are considered inflation proof because they will always pay out more than inflation thanks to that fixed rate.
The current 5.51% total rate is based on an annual fixed rate of 1.4%, the highest it's been in 20 years, and an annual variable or inflation rate of 4.08%, the highest it's been since 2022.
You are allowed to purchase up to $10,000 in electronic I Bonds each year.
Are these I Bonds worth the investment?
Chris Woods, a financial adviser and the founder of Silvis Financial, said the current rate is attractive. But he noted that with the 10-year Treasury close to 5%, you can find corporate bond funds that have a 4% to 6% return, with liquidity. I Bonds can't be redeemed during their first 12 months, and if you redeem them in less than five years, then you lose the last three months of interest.
Woods said he would consider adding them in a fixed-income portfolio as part of an intermediate (18 months to seven years) or long-term strategy (seven years or more), but there would have to be other investments in that portfolio as well.
What you should know about transitioning to Treasury Direct's new login system ID.me
Treasury Direct is the only place online where you can buy and redeem U.S. savings bonds, although you can buy other securities outside of the Treasury Direct system, like Treasury bills and notes.
Starting last week, ID.me — a third-party service — became the only method to log in to your Treasury Direct account. To gain access, you'll need to go through the ID.me setup process. Other government agencies also use ID.me, including the Internal Revenue Service and the Social Security Administration.
A FAQ on TreasuryDirect says that it's making the transition because it's "a more standardized, secure way of logging in."
"It uses a government-trusted method to verify your identity, which protects your sensitive personal and financial information from identity theft and unauthorized access," the FAQ states.
The process entails listing either your Social Security number and uploading some form of verification, which can include photos of either your license or state ID; your passport; or your passport card. Afterwards, you'll also have to take a video selfie using your phone.
Without ID.me, you won't be able to access Treasury Direct, but any previous investments you had with the Treasury “are not permanently frozen or seized,” according to the FAQ.
Is ID.me safe?
Last week, Democratic Senators Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and Ron Wyden of Oregon sent a letter to government officials raising concerns about the transition to ID.me and asked them to at least halt the implementation of the service until after the 2027 tax filing season. They recommended the use of login.gov instead.
Both senators pointed out that there may be a steeper learning curve for certain groups, including older Americans and those without modern devices, and noted that biometric matching can be inaccurate, especially for people of color. A 2019 federal study found that facial recognition systems misidentified people of color more frequently than white people.
They also referenced the IRS' transition to ID.me several years ago. At the time, Democrats in Congress were also concerned about having Americans entrust a third-party service with sensitive information, like their biometric data, and said that a biometric database would be a target for cyberattacks.
Anton Dahbura, executive director of Johns Hopkins University's Information Security Institute, said that the ID.me rollout should not deter people from buying bonds if they had already planned to.
But Dahbura said there are aspects of the service that are "murky" and should be made transparent to the public, like how exactly your information is protected and how your information is deleted.
"Using a private contractor isn't inherently a security problem, and what matters is that the government maintains strong oversight and can demonstrate that the contractor meets the rigorous security and privacy requirements for these kinds of things," he said.
Nancy Kim, a professor emerita at Illinois Tech’s Chicago-Kent College of Law, has concerns with the service and pointed out that if someone takes your biometric data, you can't change that information like you can with your password. She also said that even if you ask ID.me to delete your data, they can keep it for up to three year

articles.title: Can chip manufacturers find an alternative to helium?
articles.text:
Can chip manufacturers find an alternative to helium?
Marketplace®
Every story is an economic story
Donate
Nov 6, 2026
Can chip manufacturers find an alternative to helium?
There are other non-reactive gases out there, but they'd be far more expensive than helium.
I've Always Wondered ...by Janet Nguyen
About 30% of the world's supply of helium has been cut off since the start of the Iran War, and there's no substitute out there.
I-HWA CHENG/AFP via Getty Images
This is just one of the stories from our “I’ve Always Wondered” series, where we tackle all of your questions about the world of business, no matter how big or small. Ever wondered if recycling is worth it? Or how store brands stack up against name brands? Check out more from the series here.
Alex Duerre from Anchorage, Alaska, asks:
With AI in full swing and the war with Iran ongoing, helium access is at risk. Helium is critical to making semiconductors. How will semiconductor manufacturers address the shortage of helium? What can replace helium? Helium is a finite element.
The short answer is nothing can replace helium — or at least anything that's cost effective.
When manufacturers are making semiconductor chips, they need to draw away heat to prevent damage. Helium achieves that goal more efficiently than other gases, explained Moses Chan, a professor emeritus of physics at Penn State University.
You could use another nonreactive gas like neon, but that might be 10,000 times more expensive, Chan said. When it comes to items like party balloons, which rely on helium, you could technically get away with less of it by adding in hydrogen, he said. But Chan said if you add in too much and that balloon is next to a birthday candle, well, that could lead to an explosion.
MRI instruments also use helium, in liquid form, and you can reengineer them to recycle it, said Sophia Hayes, a chemistry professor at Washington University in St. Louis.
But there is basically no true substitute for helium in nearly all uses." You either have to replace the technology entirely with something that doesn't require helium, or you can reengineer things to use less," Hayes said.
In October, the U.S. the Department of Energy announced it would add helium to its list of critical materials, which includes substances or minerals that are both essential for energy technology and at high risk of a supply chain disruption.
When the Strait of Hormuz closed due to the Iran War, that stopped us from having access to helium produced by Qatar, which produces about 30% of the world's global supply.
Meanwhile, the demand for chips has skyrocketed as companies ramp up their investments in AI.
There used to be a Federal Helium Reserve, similar to our Strategic Petroleum Reserve, Chan pointed out. But the U.S. government sold it in 2024, a decision that had been decades in the making after lawmakers wanted to cut government spending.
So what happens in the meantime? "To the best of my knowledge, we are just trying to wait out these supply shortages," Hayes said. Hayes said she hasn't heard of any companies shutting their plants down, but they have that option.
Marketplace reached out to the Semiconductor Industry Association for an interview, but did not get a response by deadline.
Polar Semiconductor — which has a manufacturing facility in Bloomington, Minnesota — said on its website that it sources helium from three suppliers, but one has restricted allocations amid the global shortage.
Other companies have publicly stated that they're not in danger due to the shortage. SK Hynix, a semiconductor manufacturer based in South Korea, told Reuters earlier this year that it has "long secured diverse supply chains and sufficient inventory" of helium. "Therefore there is almost no chance that the company will be affected," SK Hynix continued.
There are some efforts to bolster production. Blue Spruce Operating plans to create a helium and natural gas processing plant in Wyoming, a state that produces 20% of the world's helium supply.

articles.title: Foreign governments own fewer Treasurys these days. That's pushing interest rates up
articles.text:
Treasury rates are up. An exodus of foreign buyers is one reason
Marketplace®
Every story is an economic story
Donate
Nov 6, 2026
Foreign governments own fewer Treasurys these days. That's pushing interest rates up
Foreign owners hold about half the share of U.S. government debt they did a couple decades back.
World/Internationalby Justin Ho
Download
Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images
Interest rates have been rising in this economy for a whole bunch of reasons. The Fed has raised rates, for one, to try to deal with a persistent inflation problem. The federal government’s also piling on debt. So are data center developers and tech companies. And all of that borrowing demand is pushing bond buyers to demand higher interest rates.
There are also some undercurrents that’ve been putting upward pressure on rates for a while now. One of those is an exodus of foreign buyers from U.S. government debt. Back in 2008, they owned around 60% of it. Today, it’s just 25%.
Foreign ownership of U.S. debt skyrocketed in the 1990s and the 2000s, back when the U.S. buying a ton of imports.
“Emerging markets, especially China, were seeing very strong export growth,” said Alex Wolf, global head of macro and fixed income strategy with J.P. Morgan.
As a result, Wolf said those countries were generating ever-growing dollar reserves. And those countries’ central banks needed a safe place to stash away all those dollars.
“They more or less would take that surplus, and they would just park it into Treasurys,” Wolf said.
These countries bought Treasurys because they’re one of the safest assets on the planet. They’re also easy to sell. That allowed countries to treat their dollar reserves like emergency funds, said Anusha Chari, an economics professor at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill.
“A country that is, for example, oil dependent, needs to maintain buffers of dollar reserves to purchase oil,” she said. “That is a way in which you finance imports.”
Chari said some countries were also worried about their own currencies, especially after they tanked during the Asian Financial Crisis in the late 1990s. Having extra dollars around let a country buy more of its own currency to prop up its value and maintain its exchange rate.
“Countries that maintain fixed exchange rates need a buffer of reserves, in case foreign investors want to get out of their currency,” Chari said.
But more recently, she said, countries haven’t been as concerned about supporting their currencies, because their economies have been growing.
“Countries in Asia, for example, have just become a lot more resilient,” Chari said. “And the accumulation has basically stagnated.”
Some countries have slowed down Treasury purchases, including Japan. Others have been selling Treasurys, including China and Russia.
“We see this weird state where Treasuries have lost their ‘ specialness’ within the space of dollar assets,” said Jesse Schreger, a professor at Columbia Business School.
That special role Treasurys used to play for foreign countries allowed the U.S. government to pay lower yields on its debt, since those foreign central banks that were buying it up didn’t really care about the interest rates they were getting paid.
“And so you’re willing to basically say, you know what, I’m going to earn less of a return on that asset, in order to get the convenience of being able to actually turn it into the things that they need at a moment’s notice,” Schreger said.
But now that foreign central banks don’t need to stockpile as many Treasurys, they’re starting to look more like any other financial asset.
“If you’re just another financial asset, that investors are trying to maximize your returns on, the only way in which you can induce investors to actually buy more of you is you can either get safer, or you can pay a higher yield,” Schreger said.
It doesn’t help that the federal government has been borrowing more over the past 15 years.
“Now, as the U.S. contemplates borrowing more and more, it doesn’t get to actually get that discount,” Schreger said.
Which means neither do mortgage holders, auto loan borrowers, or anyone else with a loan that’s tied to Treasury yields.

articles.title: Mara Wilson asks, should we still have child stars?
articles.text:
Mara Wilson asks, should we still have child stars?

Mara Wilson asks, should we still have child stars?
Former child star Mara Wilson on the perils of childhood fame.
Download
Actor Mara Wilson (left) and journalist Kate Taylor (right)
Mara Wilson's photo credit: Elizabeth Weinberg
Subscribe:
Apple
Spotify
Amazon
RSS
Plenty of kids dream of becoming famous actors. But with more and more former child stars coming forward about the cost of fame, is it time to rethink putting kids in front of the camera?
This week on the show, guest host Jasmine Romero is joined by actor Mara Wilson (who you might remember from “Mrs. Doubtfire” and “Matilda”) and journalist Kate Taylor to break down the state of play for child stars. Taylor wrote an exposé on Dan Schneider’s Nickelodeon shows and was an executive producer on the documentary series, “ Quiet on Set: The Dark Side of Kid’s TV.”
Child labor laws prohibit employing kids in most workplaces, but acting is one of the few exceptions. “You can't have a kid going and working in a grocery store when they're eight years old,” said Taylor. “But this is something that has been carved out for children to continue to be child actors.” And that work can take a toll as young performers face pressure to financially support their families and live up to the public’s expectations of them. “I don’t think you can be world famous and remain unscathed,” said Wilson.
A few takeaways from this episode:
The Coogan Law: The law was inspired by 1920s child star Jackie Coogan, whose parents spent nearly all of his earnings. The Coogan Law in California ensures that 15% of a child’s earnings are put in a bank account that will become accessible to the child actor when they turn 18. Wilson thinks that child actors should receive a larger share of their earnings: “If that child makes a million dollars, they are not seeing most of that money.” Taylor has spoken to former child stars who, as kids, financially supported their parents: “It complicates the parent-child relationship where it almost feels like for a kid, they are the breadwinner in the family.”
Protecting children from the media and public opinion: Thankfully, more protections are in place for child actors on set, but it’s harder to protect child stars from the wider world. “I had a press that called me an annoying spoiled brat…I had grown men who knew my name and would comment on me and my body,” said Wilson. Wilson and Taylor suggested that child actors shouldn’t have to go on press junkets, where they’re often asked invasive questions. “This is something that both puts you in the public eye and…you do not get any financial compensation,” said Taylor. “So I think that that is something that would be amazing to actually just ban for child actors.
Kids cannot understand the long-term effects of fame. As a child, Wilson asked her parents to let her audition for film and TV. But she couldn’t have known then that becoming famous would have lifelong consequences. Taylor agreed, “The parent has the responsibility to say no unless they have met everyone on this project, unless they have put a lot of guardrails into place to protect their kid...it's just opening up a whole world of possibilities that I don't think a kid can understand what they're walking into.”

ChatGPT for Teens' safeguards don't work, risk assessment finds
The chatbot was advertised as age-appropriate by OpenAI. But parental control features and study mode are easily bypassed, says Tom Siegel, executive director of the Youth AI Safety Institute at Common Sense Media.
Download
sankai/Getty Images
Subscribe:
Apple
Spotify
Amazon
RSS
OpenAI's new teen-appropriate version of ChatGPT may not be living up to its promises, according to an independent evaluation. The new mode is supposed to have stronger guardrails for sensitive topics, automatic parental alerts and a study tool that won't just give kids the answers to their homework.
But the nonprofit Common Sense Media evaluated the tool and found it poses "unacceptable risks." Tom Siegel leads the Youth Safety Institute at Common Sense and tested about 4,000 prompts using fake teen accounts. He spoke with Meghan McCarty Carino about his findings.
More on this
“ ChatGPT for Teens Poses Unacceptable Risk to Kids, Common Sense Media Finds” from Common Sense Media
An OpenAI spokesperson sent Marketplace a statement via email:
“We are deeply committed to teen safety and to developing safeguards and giving parents meaningful tools to guide their teens’ use of AI. We welcome rigorous independent evaluation, but we do not believe Common Sense Media’s testing accurately reflects how ChatGPT’s teen safeguards work in practice or expert perspectives on how AI can support teens. Our review of Common Sense Media’s methodology shows that the bulk of their testing may have begun and concluded before activation of parental controls was complete, making their findings inaccurate. If that was the case, the tests would not establish whether parental safety notifications work as designed.
We are committed to continuing to work with experts to ensure our products provide teens opportunities to learn and create and give parents confidence.”
